title: Kinematic Viscosity: cSt, SUS and ISO VG Grades
h1: Kinematic viscosity — cSt, SUS and ISO VG
description: 1 cSt = 1 mm²/s. ISO VG 32 is 32 cSt at 40 °C. SUS is a legacy timed-flow measurement. Confuse the columns and pump sizing drifts.

author.name: The Turbo Unit Converter engineering desk

reviewer.name: Turbo Unit Converter editorial review
reviewer.credential: verified against NIST SP 811 and category-specific ISO references

hero: ν = µ/ρ. Kinematic viscosity is what pipe-flow and pump-curve calculations actually take.
body: Kinematic viscosity is dynamic viscosity divided by density. It has the units of area over time. It is what Reynolds number and centrifugal pump curves are built around, and it is the number on ISO viscosity grade charts.

> 1 cSt = 1 mm²/s = 10⁻⁶ m²/s
> 1 stokes (St) = 100 cSt = 10⁻⁴ m²/s
> SUS (Saybolt Universal Seconds) is an empirical timed measurement, non-linear with cSt below 30 cSt
ISO VG 32 → 32 cSt at 40 °C, tolerance ±10%. VG 46, 68, 100, 150, 220, 320, 460 follow the R10 series. Hydraulic fluid: typically VG 32–68. Gearbox oil: VG 150–460.
Above 100 cSt: cSt ≈ SUS / 4.635. Between 30 and 100 cSt: use the ASTM D2161 table. Below 30 cSt the relationship becomes strongly non-linear — do not use a linear factor.

A pump spec calls for ISO VG 46. Fluid choice: 46 cSt at 40 °C, ~7 cSt at 100 °C. In an outdoor unit that reaches 100 °C bulk oil temperature, pump volumetric efficiency drops with viscosity — VG 46 at 100 °C is too thin, upgrade to VG 68.
cSt = mm²/s. Match ISO VG grade to operating temperature. Skip SUS unless the spec forces you into it.

faqs.q: Is cSt the same as centistokes?

faqs.a: It is a representative operating temperature for industrial hydraulics and gearboxes.
